assessments.title: A5 knowledge test
assessments.format: Two hours · paper-based MCQ, true/false and short answers. Longer short answers are likely, according to Max.
assessments.scope: A5 assesses integrated care, Te Tiriti-led culturally safe practice, health assessment and nursing interventions, health equity, and primary health care. The teaching weeks and labs provide practice context. The 2025 immunisation schedule is explicitly testable; Week 6 guidance says older-adult and cancer material may appear. Portfolio and placement assessments are separate tasks.

units.title: Primary health care
units.scope: PHC, equity, Te Tiriti, health literacy, digital empathy and community nursing
gaps: Indwelling-catheter lab detail is not captured.
IMAC pre-learning and vaccine-administration/cold-chain teaching are not captured; the separately scheduled knowledge-test material is included with its August 2025 date.

units.title: Perinatal care
units.scope: Pregnancy, postnatal assessment, infant safety and postnatal mental health
gaps: PHQ-3 recall period/scoring conflicts between supplied sources, so no numerical scoring is taught. The EPDS form establishes its screening purpose and seven-day recall period, but does not establish its use in the postnatal lab.

units.title: Child and whānau health
units.scope: First 1000 days, Well Child Tamariki Ora, development, home visiting and middle childhood
gaps: Growth-chart and infant-assessment lab materials need further review against their original chart/context sources.

units.title: Adolescence and addiction
units.scope: Youth psychosocial assessment, risk, substance use and motivational interviewing
gaps: The adolescent deck’s slide 21 lists consent, capacity and competence as headings but supplies no fuller consent framework; the deck’s capacity diagram and listed assessment abilities are represented.

units.title: Disability, dementia and wounds
units.scope: Inclusive care, communication, unmet needs, Newcastle approach and chronic wound assessment
gaps: The stated dementia/delirium/depression learning outcome is supplemented with attributed NHS/NICE sources because the supplied lecture does not teach that comparison. Wound cards cover assessment, patterns, arterial checks before compression and possible infection only; broad wound-management selection criteria remain unavailable.

units.title: Older adulthood and cancer
units.scope: Healthy ageing, holistic assessment, community services, cancer prevention and survivorship
gaps: The cancer lecture schematic labels stages 0, I and IV only; it does not teach a complete staging system. Cancer-screening statements retain their course-slide context and have not been established as current programme eligibility or guidance.

Whānau Ora Sectors involved: Health + Social Development + Education + Iwi + Justice + Housing Description: A holistic approach to health and well-being that empowers whānau to set goals and access services across sectors through a single navigator. The First 1000 Days The first 1000 days of life, from conception to age two, is the most critical developmental phase for a child's development . During this period, the brain grows rapidly, laying the foundations for cognitive and socio-emotional health. Proper nutrition, caregiver attachment and care are essential to support this growth, influencing a child's long-term health and potential. Early experiences and environment also shape social and emotional skills, which are

Proper nutrition, caregiver attachment and care are essential to support this growth, influencing a child's long-term health and potential. Early experiences and environment also shape social and emotional skills, which are crucial for future learning and well-being. Investing in these early days helps reduce health inequalities and supports optimal development, ensuring children can reach their full potential. Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) refer to traumatic events occurring between the ages of 1 and 17 that can have significant impacts on a child's development and overall health. These experiences are categorized into three main areas: abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction. Examples include domestic violence, parental separation, substance abuse, mental illness in the household, and physical or emotional neglect. ACEs are linked to toxic stress, which can disrupt brain

This side represents the length of life that can be extended through cancer treatments . It emphasizes the importance of additional time, regardless of the quality of that time. Attachment • One of the key processes involved in emotional development is attachment. • Attachment was first described by the British child psychiatrist John Bowlby as: “A strong affectional or emotional tie that binds a person to an intimate companion”

Caregiver Responsiveness: Secure attachment develops when caregivers are sensitive, available, and responsive to a child's needs, leading to positive social and emotional outcomes • Impact on Adulthood: The theory extends to adult relationships, where early attachment experiences influence patterns of interaction and emotional bonds in adult relationships

Why is attachment important? o The ability to form successful attachment relationships between individuals is essential to our ability to function and live as a social group, which is necessary for our survival as a species o The quality of the parent / child relationship has long been known to be a key factor influencing emotional, physical and cognitive outcomes as an adult o The attachment relationship helps us make sense of world o Attachment facilitates self-regulation

HOWEVER not all people with insecure attachment early in life will develop MH disorders. Environmental factors, trauma and genetic predispositions may also play a role. Interventions such as early recognition, parental guidance, therapy and safe adult relationships can mitigate outcomes.

Category A
Drugs which have been taken by a large number of pregnant women and women of childbearing age without any proven increase in the frequency of malformations or other direct or indirect harmful effects on the fetus having been observed.

Category B1
Drugs which have been taken by only a limited number of pregnant women and women of childbearing age, without an increase in the frequency of malformation or other direct or indirect harmful effects on the human fetus having been observed. Studies in animals have not shown evidence of an increased occurrence of fetal damage.

Category B2
Drugs which have been taken by only a limited number of pregnant women and women of childbearing age, without an increase in the frequency of malformation or other direct or indirect harmful effects on the human fetus having been observed. Studies in animals are inadequate or may be lacking, but available data show no evidence of an increased occurrence of fetal damage.

Category B3
Drugs which have been taken by only a limited number of pregnant women and women of childbearing age, without an increase in the frequency of malformation or other direct or indirect harmful effects on the human fetus having been observed. Studies in animals have shown evidence of an increased occurrence of fetal damage, the significance of which is considered uncertain in humans.

Category C
Drugs which, owing to their pharmacological effects, have caused or may be suspected of causing, harmful effects on the human fetus or neonate without causing malformations. These effects may be reversible.

Category D
Drugs which have caused, are suspected to have caused or may be expected to cause, an increased incidence of human fetal malformations or irreversible damage. These drugs may also have adverse pharmacological effects.

Category X
Drugs which have such a high risk of causing permanent damage to the fetus that they should not be used in pregnancy or when there is a possibility of pregnancy.
The biggest problem is the alphabetical nature of the A–X categorisation. It implies (incorrectly) that there is a hierarchy of risk with category C being “worse” than category B.

Environmental/social contributors listed include disliking the environment or other people, lack of activity, feeling alone or abandoned, staff/carer actions unintentionally causing problems, inadequate support, task-focused care, noise/crowding and unfamiliar carers.

Possible improvements include communication between staff, activity therapy, pain relief, learning the person’s background, one-to-one support, greater choice, friendlier interactions, staff training/input, slower care, reassurance and understanding causes.

Other possible improvements include consistent approaches, structure and repetition, targeted therapeutic lies, meaningful activities, better signage, outdoor access, physical investigations, improved living environment, medication changes and person-centred communication.

questions.prompt: A patient reports missed contraceptive pills and recent unprotected sex. Explain the information needed, the difference between COC and POP instructions, and when emergency contraception should be considered.
rubric: Vomiting/diarrhoea, enzyme-inducing medicines, starting late or extending a hormone-free interval can compromise exposure and contraceptive effect.

For one missed active pill, the guide says take it as soon as remembered and continue normally. For two or more, take one active pill promptly and resume; timing/regimen determines backup. In a traditional regimen, misses in the first/last active week can require seven consecutive active pills with condoms/abstinence and no extended break; consider emergency contraception after unprotected sex in the break/week one.

The guide defines a traditional norethisterone/levonorgestrel POP as missed when more than three hours late; desogestrel has a twelve-hour window. Take the missed pill promptly and continue at the usual time; the guide specifies backup for the next 48 hours and EC assessment after unprotected intercourse. Follow the exact product’s instructions.
